  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via 
<br class="ltx_break">Coupled Optimization Geometry</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Guanghui Min
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:jjm8vr@virginia.edu">jjm8vr@virginia.edu</a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tianhao Huang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, USA
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ke Wan
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, USA
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chen Chen
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Department of Computer Science, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, USA
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Targeted data selection has emerged as a crucial paradigm for efficient instruction tuning, aiming to identify a small yet influential subset of training examples for a specific target task.
In practice, influence is often measured through the effect of an example on parameter updates.
To make selection scalable, many approaches leverage optimizer statistics (e.g., Adam states) as an axis-aligned surrogate for update geometry (i.e., diagonal precondition), implicitly treating parameters as coordinate-wise independent.
We show that this assumption breaks down in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA. In this setting, the induced optimization geometry exhibits strong cross-parameter coupling with non-trivial off-diagonal interactions, while the task-relevant update directions are confined to a low-dimensional subspace.
Motivated by this mismatch, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> (<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">G</span>radient <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">I</span>sometric <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">S</span>ubspace <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">T</span>ransformation), a simple yet principled alternative that replaces axis-aligned scaling with robust subspace alignment.
<span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> recovers a task-specific subspace from validation gradients via spectral filtering (SVD), projects training gradients into this coupled subspace, and scores examples by their alignment with target directions.
Extensive experiments have demonstrated that <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> matches or outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline with only 0.29% of the storage and 25% of the computational time under the same selection budget.
Our code is available at <a href="https://github.com/GuanghuiMin/GIST" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/GuanghuiMin/GIST</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Instruction tuning has become the de facto standard for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. While early approaches relied on scaling up the volume of instruction data, recent findings have precipitated a paradigm shift: the quality and relevance of data are far more critical than mere quantity. Seminal works like LIMA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and AlpaGasus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> demonstrate that a small, carefully curated subset of high-quality examples can rival or even surpass the performance of models trained on massive, unfiltered datasets. This “less is more” phenomenon has catalyzed a surge of interest in automated data selection, aiming to identify the most effective training samples from large-scale pools to maximize downstream performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond general alignment, a more practical and challenging problem is <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Targeted Instruction Tuning</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, where the goal is to select a data subset that maximizes performance on a specific target distribution under a limited budget. Existing approaches generally fall into three categories.
First, hard example mining prioritizes training samples based on scalar metrics like perplexity or loss magnitude <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin and Rush, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Antonello et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Second, similarity-based methods utilize embedding retrieval to identify semantically relevant examples in the representation space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hanawa et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Finally, optimizer-based methods, exemplified by the state-of-the-art framework LESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, quantify data contribution directly in the gradient space via influence functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh and Liang, 2017</a>)</cite>. Notably, LESS incorporates optimization geometry by leveraging Adam states, offering a scalable solution for LLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, relying on optimizer statistics imposes a fundamental geometric limitation, prioritizing computational efficiency over the precision of the quadratic approximation.
Designed for linear scalability, optimizers like Adam approximate the local curvature, referring to the Hessian geometry describing the loss landscape, via a <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diagonal</em> preconditioner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba, 2015</a>)</cite>.
While efficient, this imposes a hard expressivity bottleneck: diagonal matrices lack the off-diagonal terms necessary to represent <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">parameter interactions</span> (e.g., the bilinear coupling in LoRA).
Consequently, this structural incapacity inevitably distorts the intrinsic metric <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amari, 1998</a>)</cite> of the parameter space.
Furthermore, Adam’s element-wise inversion indiscriminately amplifies directions with small gradients.
In the context of low-rank adaptation, where the vast majority of the parameter space constitutes a noisy null space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aghajanyan et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, this scaling boosts noise rather than preserving the sparse update structure.
Ultimately, unlike Newton’s method which leverages full curvature to identify optimal descent paths, this approximation fails to capture the true <em id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">descent potential</em> of induced updates, fundamentally misestimating their impact on loss reduction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by this mismatch, we introduce <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> (<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">G</span>radient <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">I</span>sometric <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">S</span>ubspace <span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">T</span>ransformation), a data selection framework that prioritizes geometric alignment over unstable diagonal approximations.
<span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> extracts a low-rank, task-specific subspace from validation gradients and scores training examples by projected gradient alignment, yielding an efficient selection rule that naturally respects parameter coupling without requiring full second-order information.
Our contributions are threefold:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:0.25cm;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theoretical Unification &amp; Analysis:</span> We unify prior targeted selection methods as approximations to a common geometry-aware objective, revealing that diagonal preconditioners are inherently limited under rotated low-rank coupling. We then derive a principled, tractable non-diagonal estimator using the spectral structure of target gradients.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">GIST<span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> Algorithm:</span></span> We introduce a scalable subspace-based selection method: <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> extracts a low-rank task subspace from validation gradients via SVD and ranks examples using projected gradient alignment, enabling efficient selection under coupled PEFT geometry.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Empirical Superiority:</span> Extensive experiments on <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2023</a>)</cite> demonstrate that <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> matches or outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline with only 0.29% of the storage and 25% of the computational time under the same selection budget.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Notations.</span>
We denote the large-scale instruction tuning dataset as <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}=\{\boldsymbol{z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}=\{\boldsymbol{z}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{D}|}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}_{i}=(\boldsymbol{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{y}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}_{i}=(\boldsymbol{x}_{i},\boldsymbol{y}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The Large Language Model (LLM) is denoted as <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We distinguish between the <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sample-wise loss</span> on a data instance <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}=(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝒚</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}=(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, denoted as <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>, and the <span id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">empirical risk</span> over a dataset <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, denoted as <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{S},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{S}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{S},\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{S}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>.
All notations and symbols are summarized in Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Notations and Symbols ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Problem Definition</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We formalize the targeted data selection task as a constrained bi-level optimization problem.
Our goal is to select a subset <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⊂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}\subset\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> with a cardinality constraint <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{S}|=k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{S}|=k</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\ll|\mathcal{D}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\ll|\mathcal{D}|</annotation></semantics></math> is the budget), such that the LLM trained on <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> minimizes the loss on the target distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>, following the setting in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>. Formally, this is defined as:</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproblem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_problem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproblem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Problem 1</span></span><span id="Thmproblem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Targeted Data Selection)<span id="Thmproblem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproblem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproblem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproblem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Find the optimal subset <math id="Thmproblem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> that solves the following bi-level optimization:</span></p>

</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Optimization Dynamics of Instruction Tuning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the optimization trajectory by examining the parameter update from step <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t+1</annotation></semantics></math>.
For clarity, we consider a per-sample (batch size <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=1</annotation></semantics></math>) update, and denote the instantaneous training objective at step <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>.
We study the local behavior of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> around the current parameters <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Newton’s Method.</span>
Ideally, the parameter update is derived by minimizing a local quadratic approximation of the instantaneous loss. We perform a second-order Taylor expansion of <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> around <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E2X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E2X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})+\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\top}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{t}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})+\mathbf{g}_{t}^{\top}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{t}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{t}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{t}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{t}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{t}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{2}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>
denote the gradient and Hessian, respectively. Minimizing this quadratic surrogate yields the stationarity condition <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{t}+\mathbf{H}_{t}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{t}+\mathbf{H}_{t}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=0</annotation></semantics></math> (assuming <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is locally invertible or appropriately regularized).
Solving for <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> yields the classical Newton update step:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{H}_{t}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{H}_{t}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> is the learning rate. Here, <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\mathbf{H}_{t}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\mathbf{H}_{t}^{-1}\mathbf{g}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the minimizer of the local quadratic surrogate, i.e., the <span id="S2.SS2.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">optimal second-order direction</span> under this approximation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adam Optimizer.</span>
In practice, LLMs are fine-tuned via the Adam optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba, 2015</a>)</cite>, utilizing exponential moving averages of gradient moments for adaptive updates. Structurally, the inverse second-moment term functions as a <em id="S2.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diagonal surrogate</em> for the curvature matrix to precondition the optimization steps; we provide the detailed update formulations in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Details of the Adam Optimizer and Gradient Rescaling ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Theoretical Analysis</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we analyze the data selection problem from the perspective of influence functions and optimization geometry. We first establish a unified view connecting data selection to gradient preconditioning. We then scrutinize standard approximations in prior work, specifically diagonal preconditioners from optimizer states, and demonstrate their theoretical failure modes in data selection. Finally, we derive a principled, tractable non-diagonal estimator based on the spectral structure revealed by target gradients.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We aim to select a training sample <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> such that training on it maximizes the reduction in the validation risk <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math>.
To quantify the effect of one-step parameter update on <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we perform a first-order Taylor expansion of the validation loss <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> around the current parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1})\approx\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})+\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}.\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1})\approx\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})+\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}.\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Ideally, using a Hessian-preconditioned local update as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh and Liang (2017)</a></cite>, the one-step change of the validation loss can be approximated by substituting a preconditioned update <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> into the first-order expansion. In particular, taking <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}\approx-\eta\,\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}\approx-\eta\,\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> yields</p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1})-\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1})-\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\approx-\eta\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\approx-\eta\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{2}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{2}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            When <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> is singular or ill-conditioned (typical for over-parameterized models), we use the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> (which is same with <math id="footnote1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> when <math id="footnote1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> is invertible). Equivalently, <math id="footnote1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> yields the minimum-norm solution to <math id="footnote1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=-\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}=-\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and ignores directions in the null space.</span></span></span>
This matrix characterizes the instantaneous curvature of the target task manifold.
For a subset <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S\subseteq\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S\subseteq\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, we add the per-sample contributions due to linearity of empirical risk, yielding:</p>
