<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Single-level Approximate Optimization)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fix the current parameters <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝛉</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under the first-order approximation,
Problem <a href="#Thmproblem1" title="Problem 1 (Targeted Data Selection). ‣ 2.1 Problem Definition ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> is approximately reduced to maximizing the predicted reduction in validation loss:</span></p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E7X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E7X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\max_{S\subseteq\mathcal{D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></munder><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\max_{S\subseteq\mathcal{D}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E7X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E7Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E7Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{s.t.}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">s.t.</mtext><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{s.t.}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E7Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle|S|=k," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle|S|=k,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">up to constants independent of <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and higher-order terms.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A full proof is provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>. Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> reveals a geometric view of targeted data selection:
each candidate subset <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is scored by alignment under the metric induced by <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> between the target gradient
<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>
and the subset gradient <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Crucially, this metric implies that selection should target the the optimal local update direction under the target metric (the Newton-type step) governed by the true parameter geometry, rather than relying on efficiency-driven optimizer statistics which often trade geometric fidelity for computational speed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In modern LLM fine-tuning, however, forming <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> (let alone <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math>) is intractable.
Consequently, existing selection criteria can be viewed as optimizing Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>)
under different structural surrogates of <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> and/or simplified assumptions about the gradient geometry,
which we formalize next.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hard Example Mining (Assumption: Magnitude Prior).</span>
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val},t}\triangleq(\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger})^{1/2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val},t}\triangleq(\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger})^{1/2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>
and <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t}(S)\triangleq(\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger})^{1/2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{t}(S)\triangleq(\mathbf{H}_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger})^{1/2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then we have</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E8X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})=\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mtext>val,t</mtext><mo>†</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext>val</mtext><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{\nabla}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(S,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})=\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E8Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E8Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\|\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}}\|_{2}\,\|\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}\|_{2}\cos\angle(\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\|\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}}\|_{2}\,\|\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}\|_{2}\cos\angle(\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.3" class="ltx_p">Hard-example mining <em id="S3.SS1.p4.3.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">implicitly assumes</em> that the directional term
<math id="S3.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos\angle(\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\angle(\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{\text{val}},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S})</annotation></semantics></math> varies little across candidate subsets (or is weakly informative),
so maximizing the influence is approximated by maximizing the magnitude <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>S</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_{S}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In practice, hard-mining ranks individual samples by length of tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or perplexity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin and Rush, 2025</a>)</cite> as a proxy for <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{g}(\boldsymbol{z})\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐠</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{g}(\boldsymbol{z})\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,
and then forms <math id="S3.SS1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> from top-ranked samples.
For cross-entropy losses, low predicted probability on the ground-truth token(s) yields both larger loss and larger output-layer residuals, which typically increases the backpropagated gradient norm under mild smoothness/bounded-Jacobian conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Similarity-based Methods (Assumption: Representation Kernel Matching).</span>
Embedding- or retrieval-based methods like RDS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hanawa et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and RDS+ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al., 2025</a>)</cite> <em id="S3.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">implicitly assume</em> that the utility/influence in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) can be well-approximated by a similarity kernel defined on a chosen representation (e.g., last-layer hidden states or external embedding models).
Equivalently, they replace the <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mtext>val,t</mtext><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math>-induced parameter-space alignment in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>)
with a representation-space kernel score and select nearest neighbors of <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> under this kernel.
This bypasses explicit modeling of the parameter-space metric induced by <math id="S3.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mtext>val,t</mtext><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> and induces a geometry determined by the chosen representation/kernel,
which may miss task-relevant anisotropy present in parameter space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Optimizer-based Methods (Assumption: Locally Orthogonal Parameter Coordinates).</span>
Scalable influence approximations, such as LESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, <em id="S3.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">implicitly assume</em> that the local metric induced by <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mtext>val,t</mtext><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> is approximately diagonal in the chosen parameter coordinates,
i.e., cross-parameter couplings are negligible and the coordinates are (locally) orthogonal under this metric.
Concretely, they use a diagonal surrogate of the form <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}}+\epsilon)^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}}+\epsilon)^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. (<a href="#A4.E22" title="Equation 22 ‣ D.1 Standard Adam Update Rule ‣ Appendix D Details of the Adam Optimizer and Gradient Rescaling ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>) derived from optimizer statistics (e.g., Adam’s second-moment estimates).
While this captures element-wise rescaling, it discards off-diagonal correlations in <math id="S3.SS1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mtext>val,t</mtext><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\text{val,t}}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> and thus cannot represent cross-parameter interactions encoded by curvature, which can change the ranking of utilities when off-diagonal correlations are non-negligible.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>The Limitation: Diagonal Surrogates Cannot Handle Coupling</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">State-of-the-art methods like LESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite> typically approximate the optimization geometry using diagonal preconditioners derived from optimizer states (e.g., Adam). This approach implicitly assumes that parameters are coordinate-wise independent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.2 The Limitation: Diagonal Surrogates Cannot Handle Coupling ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that the validation-gradient matrix concentrates most of its variance
in a low-dimensional principal subspace (rapid spectral decay and early saturation of explained variance),
a consequence of the targeted setting where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val}})\leq|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}|\ll d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>rank</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≪</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val}})\leq|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}|\ll d</annotation></semantics></math>.
Importantly, <em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low-rank does not imply axis-alignment</em>. The resulting principal directions are generally
<em id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">linear combinations</em> of coordinates, i.e., a rotated subspace that encodes genuine parameter coupling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We show that coupling in PEFT is structural rather than incidental.
Under LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> with <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=W_{0}+BA" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=W_{0}+BA</annotation></semantics></math>, even a local quadratic model in <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> produces <em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">off-diagonal</em> curvature in LoRA parameter space (Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 3.2 (LoRA induces off-diagonal curvature). ‣ 3.2 The Limitation: Diagonal Surrogates Cannot Handle Coupling ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.2</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(LoRA induces off-diagonal curvature)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(W)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(W)</annotation></semantics></math> be twice differentiable and consider the LoRA parameterization <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W=W_{0}+BA" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W=W_{0}+BA</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{W}=\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{vec}(W)}\mathcal{L}(W)|_{W=W_{0}+BA}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∇</mo><mrow><mi>vec</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{W}=\nabla^{2}_{\mathrm{vec}(W)}\mathcal{L}(W)|_{W=W_{0}+BA}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For any <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in[r]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in[r]</annotation></semantics></math> and any <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j_{1}\neq j_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j_{1}\neq j_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial A_{kj_{1}}\partial A_{kj_{2}}}=(B_{:k}\otimes e_{j_{1}})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{W}(B_{:k}\otimes e_{j_{2}})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mo>∂</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial A_{kj_{1}}\partial A_{kj_{2}}}=(B_{:k}\otimes e_{j_{1}})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{W}(B_{:k}\otimes e_{j_{2}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="B_{:k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{:k}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th column of <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is the standard basis vector.
In particular, whenever the <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>-space curvature couples coordinates <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> along a nonzero direction <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m13" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="B_{:k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{:k}</annotation></semantics></math>,
the LoRA-parameter Hessian contains a nonzero off-diagonal entry.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 3.2 (LoRA induces off-diagonal curvature). ‣ 3.2 The Limitation: Diagonal Surrogates Cannot Handle Coupling ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> shows that coupling is not an artifact of optimization noise:
it is <em id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">structurally induced</em> by the bilinear parameterization <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="BA" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>A</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">BA</annotation></semantics></math> and manifests as genuine off-diagonal curvature
in LoRA parameter space. The full proof is provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Geometrically, a diagonal preconditioner can only <em id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rescale</em> coordinate axes; it cannot represent the
<em id="S3.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">rotation/shear</em> encoded by off-diagonal curvature. Concretely, even in 2D, if
<math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}=\begin{bmatrix}1&amp;\rho\\
\rho&amp;1\end{bmatrix}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd><mtd><mi>ρ</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mi>ρ</mi></mtd><mtd><mn>1</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}=\begin{bmatrix}1&amp;\rho\\
\rho&amp;1\end{bmatrix}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho\neq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho\neq 0</annotation></semantics></math>,
then for any diagonal <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(d_{1},d_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐃</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(d_{1},d_{2})</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{D}\|_{F}^{2}=(1-d_{1})^{2}+(1-d_{2})^{2}+2\rho^{2}\;\geq\;2\rho^{2}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐃</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn> 2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>ρ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{D}\|_{F}^{2}=(1-d_{1})^{2}+(1-d_{2})^{2}+2\rho^{2}\;\geq\;2\rho^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">so a diagonal surrogate suffers an irreducible error floor whenever curvature is rotated/coupled.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.F1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Spectral analysis of the <span id="S3.F1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> validation gradient <math id="S3.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> on Llama2-7B. We decompose the gradient matrix via SVD to obtain singular values <math id="S3.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. <span id="S3.F1.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> Cumulative explained variance. A steeper curve indicates that a <span id="S3.F1.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">smaller principal subspace dimension</span> is sufficient to capture the majority of the variance (e.g., Rank <math id="S3.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> captures <math id="S3.F1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>95</mn><mo mathsize="1.110em">%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">95\%</annotation></semantics></math>), confirming high directional information density. <span id="S3.F1.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> The singular values (<math id="S3.F1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{k}</annotation></semantics></math>) exhibit precipitous decay, further verifying the intrinsic low-rank structure.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 The Limitation: Diagonal Surrogates Cannot Handle Coupling ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> suggests that diagonal surrogates cannot represent the rotated, coupled geometry that governs targeted improvement.
Thus, rather than refining a diagonal scaling, we construct a tractable <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">non-diagonal</em> operator that captures cross-parameter couplings while remaining computable at LLM scale.
In the ideal influence proxy (Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>)), the metric <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> measures alignment between the target gradient and a candidate update, but forming <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> (let alone <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math>) is infeasible.
Crucially, for ranking data we do not need an entrywise approximation of <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math>; it suffices to recover a low-dimensional <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">coupled subspace</em> that concentrates the dominant task-relevant directions, which diagonal methods cannot express by construction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our construction starts from per-example validation gradients, which are already required to define the targeted direction.
Let <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}|\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}|\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> be the stacked gradient matrix whose rows are <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>val</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Define the gradient covariance proxy</p>
<table id="S3.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\ \triangleq\ \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.778em" rspace="0.778em">≜</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.778em">∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\ \triangleq\ \mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{d\times d},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">which is <em id="S3.SS3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">positive semidefinite (PSD)</em> and <em id="S3.SS3.p2.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">non-diagonal</em>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/gist_pipeline.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:390/78;" width="390" height="78"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of <span id="S3.F2.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>.<span id="S3.F2.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
</span>Step 1: Lightweight warmup<span id="S3.F2.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> performs a short LoRA warmup on a sampled subset and computes validation gradients.
</span>Step 2: Spectral filtering<span id="S3.F2.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> applies an SVD on the validation gradient matrix to construct a low-rank target subspace (Target projector).
</span>Step 3: Geometric scoring<span id="S3.F2.8.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> projects candidate gradients onto the target subspace and selects Top-<math id="S3.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> samples.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.3</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Eigenspace stability of the proxy)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{M})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{M})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the top-<math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> eigenspace of a PSD matrix <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐌</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the principal-angle matrix between two subspaces.
For negative log-likelihood (NLL) objectives, the per-example Hessian admits the classical Gauss–Newton/Fisher decomposition, and there exists a quantity <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{t}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{t}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>
that summarizes (i) the residual-curvature magnitude and (ii) the proxy mismatch, such that</span></p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}),\ \mathcal{S}_{r}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\big)\big\|_{2}\ \leq\ C\,\varepsilon_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.778em" rspace="0.778em">≤</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}),\ \mathcal{S}_{r}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\big)\big\|_{2}\ \leq\ C\,\varepsilon_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where the constant <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> depends only on the leading eigengap of the validation curvature.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A full proof and formal conditions are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>.
Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> implies that exact entrywise matching is unnecessary; instead, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">it suffices for the loss to decrease to a low magnitude</span> to bound the subspace approximation error.
This insight elucidates the requirement of a warm-up phase: it is required to steer the optimization trajectory out of the initial high-noise regime into a local basin where the curvature stabilizes.
Crucially, since pre-trained models facilitate a rapid initial descent, this warm-up can be <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">extremely brief</span>.
Empirical validation of these dynamics is provided in Appendix <a href="#A9.SS2" title="I.2 Warmup and Training Dynamics of LoRA Finetuning ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We therefore recover the task subspace directly from <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> via a compact SVD:</p>
<table id="S3.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
