</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">and define the rank-<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> projector <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{r}\triangleq\mathbf{V}_{t,r}\mathbf{V}_{t,r}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{r}\triangleq\mathbf{V}_{t,r}\mathbf{V}_{t,r}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> using the top-<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> right singular vectors.
By Eckart–Young–Mirsky <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eckart and Young, 1936</a>)</cite>, <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> is the optimal rank-<math id="S3.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> linear operator for capturing the dominant variation of <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> under squared reconstruction error.
Importantly, <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> is explicitly non-diagonal: it represents a rotation in parameter space and can encode the coupled directions that diagonal preconditioners provably miss, yielding a tractable surrogate geometry for comparing candidate updates in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>: The Proposed Methodology</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Based on the theoretical analysis in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we propose <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>, a data selection framework that leverages spectral subspace filtering to robustly identify high-value training samples. <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> operates in three main steps: (1) capturing gradient trajectories via lightweight LoRA warmup, (2) extracting the intrinsic target geometry via SVD, and (3) selecting data based on projected alignment. Full pipeline is illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Subspace Gradient Feature Computation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 1: Trajectory Collection via Lightweight Warmup.</span>
To efficiently approximate the evolution of the optimization landscape without incurring the cost of full training, we perform a lightweight warmup.
We randomly sample a small subset of the candidate pool (e.g., <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\%</annotation></semantics></math>), denoted as <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>⊂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, and fine-tune the base LLM on <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> using LoRA adapters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> for an epoch.
We collect the checkpoint <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> denote the number of trainable LoRA parameters. For each target example <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> and candidate example <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒛</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}\in\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute their gradients <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> in the LoRA parameter space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 2: Extracting the Task Subspace.</span>
Construct the target gradient matrix <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\text{val},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\text{val},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then we perform Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\text{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\text{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\text{val},t}=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐔</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\text{val},t}=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">We determine the effective rank <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> by analyzing the singular value spectrum (e.g., capturing 95% explained variance).
The <span id="S4.SS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Target Projector</span> is then defined by the top-<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> right singular vectors:</p>
<table id="S4.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Pi}\triangleq\mathbf{V}_{r}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝚷</mi><mo>≜</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐕</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Pi}\triangleq\mathbf{V}_{r}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">This operator captures the principal directions of the task while discarding the orthogonal noise.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step 3: Geometric Scoring via Projected Alignment.</span>
Let <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{\text{val},t}^{(j)}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐠</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{\text{val},t}^{(j)}\triangleq\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. With the target projector <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚷</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Pi}</annotation></semantics></math>, we map gradients into the <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional target subspace.
For a candidate <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and a specific target example <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define their <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subspace Alignment Score</span> at step <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> as the cosine similarity of their projected gradients:</p>
<table id="S4.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)})\triangleq\frac{(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{i,t})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{\text{val},t}^{(j)})}{\|\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{i,t}\|_{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{\text{val},t}^{(j)}\|_{2}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext>Sim</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝚷</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝚷</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐠</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝚷</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝚷</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐠</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)})\triangleq\frac{(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{i,t})^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{\text{val},t}^{(j)})}{\|\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{i,t}\|_{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{g}_{\text{val},t}^{(j)}\|_{2}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Note that <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{i}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{i}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell(\boldsymbol{z}_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> aggregates token-level contributions (average over tokens), so its norm can vary substantially with sequence length and local loss scale.
To prevent such magnitude effects from dominating the ranking, we use cosine similarity after projecting to the learned task subspace: normalization removes per-example scale variations, while <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚷</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Pi}</annotation></semantics></math> retains only the coupled directions that are reproducible on <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As a result, <span id="S4.SS1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> scores candidates by directional agreement with the target geometry, rather than by raw gradient inner product that can be confounded by token aggregation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Multi-Task Aggregation and Selection</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In standard setting, the target set <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}=\{\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(M)}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}=\{\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(M)}\}</annotation></semantics></math> is constructed such that each example represents a distinct task or capability.
A candidate data point might be highly relevant to one specific task (e.g., math) but orthogonal to others (e.g., coding). Averaging the target gradients
would dilute these specific gradient directions.
Instead, we employ a <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Maximum Relevance</span> strategy, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al. (2025)</a></cite>. For each candidate <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{z}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{z}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute its alignment with every target example <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j\in\{1,\dots,M\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j\in\{1,\dots,M\}</annotation></semantics></math> using Eq. (<a href="#S4.E16" title="Equation 16 ‣ 4.1 Subspace Gradient Feature Computation ‣ 4 GIST: The Proposed Methodology ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>) and retain the maximum score:</p>
<table id="S4.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FinalScore}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i})=\max_{j\in\{1,\dots,M\}}\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>FinalScore</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mtext>Sim</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝒛</mi><mtext>val</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FinalScore}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i})=\max_{j\in\{1,\dots,M\}}\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\text{val}}^{(j)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This strategy prioritizes <em id="S4.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">specialist</em> candidates that effectively support at least one target requirement, regardless of their utility for others.
Finally, we select the top-<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidates with the highest FinalScore for fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Datasets.</span> We adopt the settings from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite> and utilize a heterogeneous pool of instruction tuning data, comprising approximately 270K examples. The pool integrates (1) task-specific datasets aggregated from sources like <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">flan v2</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Longpre et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">cot</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, with (2) open-ended, human-authored generation datasets such as <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">dolly</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conover et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">open assistant 1</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Köpf et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. These sources exhibit significant variance in both instruction format and underlying reasoning logic. We note that this pool is designed to be disjoint from the target domain, ensuring that the selection process is tested in a rigorous transfer setting. See Appendix <a href="#A7.SS1" title="G.1 Training Datasets ‣ Appendix G Training ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.1</span></a> for additional details.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">

We select tasks covering diverse output formats, including multiple-choice, extractive spans, and generative reasoning.</span></figcaption>

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation datasets.</span>
Following the evaluation protocol established by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we benchmark our method on three diverse datasets: <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clark et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> serves as a broad knowledge test, covering 57 subjects ranging from elementary mathematics to law.
<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> evaluates multilingual reading comprehension across 9 typologically diverse languages, requiring the model to extract exact answers from passages.
<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> is a curated suite of 27 challenging tasks from BIG-Bench, designed to probe complex reasoning capabilities.
Table <a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> provides detailed statistics.
Consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>, we utilize the few-shot examples provided in each subtask for a dual purpose: they serve as the target set <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> to guide our data selection and subsequently act as in-context demonstrations during evaluation. See Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Evaluation ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> for further details.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models for data selection and training.</span>
We evaluate <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> with three representative base models: Llama2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, Llama3.2-3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubey et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and Qwen2.5-1.5B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team, 2024</a>)</cite>.
Following standard efficient fine-tuning protocols, all training stages are conducted using LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
We report the average performance and standard deviation across three random seeds.
Appendix <a href="#A7.SS3" title="G.3 Training Details ‣ Appendix G Training ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a> provides further implementation details.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> against methods spanning four categories. First, as a naive baseline, we employ <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random Selection</span>. Second, we evaluate heuristics prioritizing intrinsic difficulty, including <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Length</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PPL.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin and Rush, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Antonello et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, where we select examples with the <em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">highest</em> perplexity. Third, we include similarity-based retrievers targeting semantic proximity to the validation set: standard <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding</span> similarity via GTR-Base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RDS+</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which exploits the model’s own hidden states. Finally, we compare against <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LESS</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, the state-of-the-art optimizer-based method selecting data via gradient projection and Adam-state rescaling. See Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Baseline Details ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> for details.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.T2.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accuracy across datasets and models. <span id="S5.T2.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Base</span> denotes 0% (no selection) and <span id="S5.T2.12.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Full</span> denotes 100% (full dataset). All other methods select 5% of the data under the same finetuning budget. Gray <math id="S5.T2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> values report standard deviations. <span id="S5.T2.12.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bold</span> numbers denote the best selected subset in each row, and <span id="S5.T2.12.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underlined</span> numbers denote the second best selected subset. Avg. <math id="S5.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math> reports the average absolute improvement over <span id="S5.T2.12.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Base</span> over <span id="S5.T2.12.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span>, <span id="S5.T2.12.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> and <span id="S5.T2.12.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span>.</span></figcaption>
<div id="S5.T2.13" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:499.5pt;height:135.4pt;vertical-align:-66.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-44.1pt,12.0pt) scale(0.8,0.8) ;">

<td id="S5.T2.13.1.13.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">–</td>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Results are reported in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Baselines ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. For LESS, following the official default setting, we run 4 epochs with random projection dimension 8192. For <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>, we run 1 warmup epoch, and use projection dimensions 150, 9, and 50 for <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span>, <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span>, and <span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span>, respectively. Gradient spectral analysis and rank selection are detailed in Appendix <a href="#A9.SS1" title="I.1 Gradient Spectrum Analysis ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">GIST<span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> matches or outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline across diverse model architectures.</span></span>
As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Baselines ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> achieves the greatest average improvement (Avg. <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta</annotation></semantics></math>) across all three models, outperforming heuristic baselines and the previous SOTA method, LESS. On Llama2-7B, <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> achieves a +6.2 average improvement, matching the Full fine-tuning upper bound.
The advantage is still pronounced on the more capable Llama3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-1.5B models, where <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> delivers improvements of +4.5 and +1.5, respectively, surpassing LESS (which achieves +3.3 and +1.1).
This demonstrates that <span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>’s geometric subspace approach can scale effectively to modern, stronger base models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">GIST<span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> validates “less is more” by surpassing fine-tuning on the full dataset</span></span>.
A remarkable finding is that <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>, using only 5% of the data, frequently matches or exceeds the performance of fine-tuning on the full dataset (100%). Specifically, on Llama3.2-3B, <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> outperforms Full fine-tuning by a substantial margin (+4.5 vs. +3.3), and on Qwen2.5-1.5B, it achieves nearly double the gain of the full dataset (+1.5 vs. +0.9). This indicates that the full dataset likely contains redundant or noisy samples that hinder optimization, whereas <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> isolates task-relevant update directions, allowing the model to learn more effectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">GIST<span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> demonstrates superior robustness compared to heuristic and optimizer-based baselines.</span></span>
While heuristics like <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Length</span> occasionally perform well on specific metrics (e.g., <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> on Llama3.2), they lack consistency, often degrading performance on other tasks (e.g., negative average gains on Qwen). Similarly, while LESS generally performs well, it struggles on Qwen2.5-1.5B, degrading on <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> (43.2 vs. Base 43.8). In contrast, <span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> maintains significant positive gains across all tasks and models, proving that subspace alignment is a more robust proxy for Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) than curvature-based influence or simple surface statistics.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Sensitivity</h3>

<figure id="S5.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F3.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/single_epoch_performance.svg" id="S5.F3.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/412;" width="476" height="412"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S5.F3.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Single Epoch Performance</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F3.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/cumulative_performance.svg" id="S5.F3.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/412;" width="476" height="412"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S5.F3.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Cumulative Performance</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Impact of Checkpoint Selection.<span id="S5.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
(a) Using single-epoch gradients shows a clear performance drop in later epochs.
(b) Aggregating multiple checkpoints (weighted) does not outperform the early-stop strategy, confirming that early gradients contain the essential task optimization directions.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Using only early checkpoints is sufficient; later checkpoints can even hurt performance.</span>
Our findings offer a nuanced perspective on checkpoint aggregation compared to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>. While aggregating influence scores can effectively stabilize the zig-zagging Adam trajectory near convergence (illustrated in Figure <a href="#A4.F5.sf2" title="Figure 5(b) ‣ Figure 5 ‣ D.2 Toy Example: Diagonal vs. Full-Matrix Preconditioning under Coupling ‣ Appendix D Details of the Adam Optimizer and Gradient Rescaling ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5(b)</span></a>), we observe that for geometric subspace alignment, <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">the most valuable directional information is intrinsically concentrated in the early training stage</span>.
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S5.F3.sf1" title="Figure 3(a) ‣ Figure 3 ‣ 5.4 Sensitivity ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(a)</span></a>, the performance of data selection using single-epoch gradients shows a monotonic decline on <span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> with Llama3.2-3B, dropping from 69.2% (Epoch 1) to 64.3% (Epoch 4).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S5.T3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Number of checkpoints (<math id="S5.T3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>) used for select data with <span id="S5.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> for Llama3.2-3B.</span></figcaption>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Even when aggregating checkpoints using the weighted scheme proposed in LESS (Figure <a href="#S5.F3.sf2" title="Figure 3(b) ‣ Figure 3 ‣ 5.4 Sensitivity ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3(b)</span></a>), adding later checkpoints yields diminishing returns and eventually harms performance: while combining Epochs 1-2 yields a slight peak (70.2%), incorporating all four epochs degrades accuracy to 67.3%, significantly lower than using the early checkpoints alone. This aligns with the results in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Sensitivity ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
We attribute this phenomenon to the evolution of the gradient geometry shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.2 The Limitation: Diagonal Surrogates Cannot Handle Coupling ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. As training progresses, the spectral distribution of the target gradient matrix becomes increasingly concentrated on the leading singular values. This shrinkage in intrinsic dimension suggests that late-stage gradients may lose the diverse directional information present in early checkpoints, discarding critical optimization directions required for robust data selection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/svd_rank.svg" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:457/195;" width="457" height="195"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.F4.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Accuracy as a function of the projection rank used by <span id="S5.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>, compared with LESS at the same selection budget.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spectral filtering is essential, yet identifying the dominant optimization direction is the primary driver of performance.</span>
Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 Sensitivity ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents the sensitivity analysis of <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> regarding subspace rank <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> on <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> (<math id="S5.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=285" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>285</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=285</annotation></semantics></math>).
We observe that performance does not increase monotonically with rank; instead, it peaks at <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=150</annotation></semantics></math> (62.9%) and drops to 62.5% using full rank (<math id="S5.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=285" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>285</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=285</annotation></semantics></math>). This confirms the necessity of spectral filtering to exclude noisy tail components that may harm generalization.
Surprisingly, even at an extremely low rank <math id="S5.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=10</annotation></semantics></math> which captures only 40% of the cumulative explained variance, <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> achieves an accuracy of 62.1%, comparable to LESS.
This further validates our core idea: effective data selection depends on <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">maintaining directional consistency with task subspace</span> instead of preserving the exact inner products of gradients. We include a detailed subspace analysis in Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Target Set Subspace Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Efficiency</h3>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compared to LESS, <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> is highly efficient in practice, achieving better performance with only about one-quarter of LESS’s wall-clock runtime for a single task.</span> Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.5 Efficiency ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> summarizes the asymptotic complexity and wall-clock runtime of each stage in <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> compared with LESS. All wall-clock time is measured in <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">single</span> A100 (80GB) GPU hours. Similar to LESS, the dominant cost comes from computing per-example gradient features, which scales linearly with the candidate dataset size <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}|</annotation></semantics></math> and the per-step training cost. In practice, <span id="S5.SS5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> is substantially cheaper overall because it requires only <em id="S5.SS5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">one</em> epoch (i.e., a single checkpoint) to form the target geometry, whereas LESS typically aggregates gradients across multiple epochs/checkpoints; this yields an end-to-end runtime that is roughly <math id="S5.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\sim 4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 4\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller under the same setup.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The target SVD is cheap to compute in <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>. </span>A key additional cost unique to <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> is the <em id="S5.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">target SVD</em> used to construct the low-rank projector. Importantly, this step is inexpensive in both theory and practice. Concretely, we avoid forming any <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\times d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\times d</annotation></semantics></math> matrix and instead compute the Gram matrix on the target set, followed by an eigendecomposition on an <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|\times|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|\times|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|</annotation></semantics></math> matrix (with chunked multiplication), so the compute primarily scales with the small target size <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|</annotation></semantics></math> and the chosen rank <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>. Empirically, constructing the projection is fast: for <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> with <math id="S5.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=9</annotation></semantics></math>, it takes only 3.51s on average; for <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> (<math id="S5.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=69" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>69</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=69</annotation></semantics></math>) and <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> (<math id="S5.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=285" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>285</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=285</annotation></semantics></math>), the average time is 22.54s and 61.06s, respectively. This confirms that the target-SVD overhead is negligible compared to gradient feature computation, and the overall runtime improvement of <span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> mainly comes from using a single-epoch gradient store.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Efficiency comparison between <span id="S5.T4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> (Ours) and LESS. Runtime is measured in <span id="S5.T4.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">single A100 GPU hours</span>. <span id="S5.T4.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> significantly reduces the overhead in Warmup and Feature Extraction stages (approx. <math id="S5.T4.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup) and requires negligible time for SVD.</span></figcaption>

</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">GIST<span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_serif"> is extremely storage-efficient in practice.</span></span>
For example, when storing gradient features for Qwen2.5-1.5B over the three tasks, <span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> uses only 217MB on disk, while LESS requires 75GB under the same setting, i.e., <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\approx 350\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>350</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 350\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger storage (about <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="99.7\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>99.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">99.7\%</annotation></semantics></math> more disk usage).
We follow the standard LESS setup with four training datasets totaling <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 270\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>270</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 270\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> examples and a projection dimension of 8192.
In contrast to LESS, which applies a Johnson–Lindenstrauss random projection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Johnson et al., 1984</a>)</cite> with entries drawn from a Rademacher distribution and stores the resulting projected gradient features across multiple checkpoints, <span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> performs a lightweight target SVD to recover a very low-dimensional task-relevant subspace and then projects gradients onto this target subspace. Together with single-epoch extraction, this leads to a dramatically smaller disk footprint.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we presented a unified optimization perspective on data selection, revealing that prior methods fundamentally suffer from geometric misalignment—either by ignoring curvature or relying on restrictive diagonal approximations. We demonstrated that in PEFT, the optimization landscape exhibits a rotated, low-rank structure that diagonal preconditioners fail to capture. To address this, we proposed <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>, which leverages spectral filtering to recover the coupled task geometry. <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced computational overhead, validating that correctly modeling optimization geometry, rather than merely scaling up selection complexity, is key to efficient targeted instruction tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper studies influence-based data selection for targeted instruction tuning of large language models, with the goal of improving data efficiency and training effectiveness. The primary intended benefits are reduced compute and cost for fine-tuning, faster iteration, and better performance on specified target tasks or domains.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our methods may also introduce or amplify risks. Because influence scores prioritize examples that most affect a chosen target set, they can reinforce target-set biases, overfit to narrow benchmarks, or de-emphasize underrepresented groups and topics if the target distribution is skewed. In addition, data selection can inadvertently increase the presence of toxic, copyrighted, private, or otherwise sensitive content if such examples are deemed influential for the target objective. These concerns are not unique to our approach but are particularly relevant when automating dataset curation.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate these risks, we recommend pairing influence-based selection with standard data governance practices, including privacy and licensing checks, toxicity and safety filtering, and audits of demographic and topical coverage. We also encourage reporting target-set construction, selection criteria, and downstream evaluation beyond the target benchmarks (e.g., robustness and safety) to reduce the chance of unintended harms.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, this work aims to advance machine learning methodology, and its broader impacts will depend on how the selected data and resulting models are deployed and governed.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Limitations and Future Work</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> offers a principled geometric view, our current instantiation is intentionally simple—a minimal, proof-driven realization of the theory. Empirically, we find that applying <span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> early in training (after a lightweight warmup) is often most beneficial; in our experiments, using it within the first two epochs can yield stronger performance. Developing more expressive variants and adaptive mechanisms that automatically decide <em id="A1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">when</em> and <em id="A1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> to apply <span id="A1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> remains an important direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Granularity and Magnitude.</span>
First, following standard practices in efficient data selection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nikdan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we utilize sequence-level gradients and cosine similarity.
While computationally robust, this choice emphasizes <span id="A1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">directional alignment</span> and de-emphasizes gradient magnitude (a proxy for difficulty) as well as token-level granularity.
As a result, <span id="A1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> may under-separate samples whose gradients share similar directions but differ substantially in scale, and token-level signals are averaged out within each sequence representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Warmup Requirement.</span>
Second, our approximation relies on the Gauss–Newton decomposition (Lemma <a href="#A5.Thmtheorem2" title="Lemma E.2 (Gauss–Newton/Fisher decomposition for NLL ( , )). ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>), which is most accurate once optimization enters a relatively stable regime.
We satisfy this with a short warmup phase.
While our experiments suggest the relevant subspace stabilizes quickly, our current analysis does not yet characterize the transient dynamics in the very early optimization steps <em id="A1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">before</em> warmup, which could potentially be leveraged for further gains.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scale vs. Direction.</span>
Third, unlike optimizer-based approaches that implicitly capture curvature scale (e.g., Adam’s second moment), <span id="A1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> focuses on recovering <span id="A1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">principal directions</span> (an eigenspace).
This is a deliberate design to avoid numerical issues associated with ill-conditioned curvature in LLMs.
However, how to incorporate reliable <em id="A1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">scaling</em> for the recovered directions (e.g., via lightweight diagonal or low-rank scale estimates) remains open.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Future Directions.</span>
Motivated by the above trade-offs, future work includes:
(1) improving the fidelity of the recovered subspace (e.g., reducing information loss introduced by spectral filtering), and
(2) developing principled and practical estimators for the effective dimensionality and stage-dependent geometry of the optimization manifold.
A deeper understanding of what dominant optimization directions represent may further inform data selection and related downstream interventions grounded in optimization geometry.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Extended Discussion on Related Work</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Instruction Data Selection.</span> The transition from data quantity to quality has become a central theme in LLM training. Early work focused on heuristic filtering based on surface-level metrics like perplexity or instruction length <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. While efficient, these methods are often <span id="A2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">task-agnostic</span>, ignoring the specific requirements of the target distribution. To address this, similarity-based approaches utilize embedding retrieval to select data semantically close to the target <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. However, semantic similarity in the pre-trained embedding space does not necessarily translate to gradient alignment during fine-tuning. Our work targets the more rigorous <span id="A2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gradient-based</span> setting, aiming to select data that explicitly optimizes the training objective on a target domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scalable Influence Approximations.</span> Influence functions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koh and Liang, 2017</a>)</cite> provide a principled framework for data selection by estimating the effect of removing a sample on validation loss. However, the classical formulation requires inverting the Hessian matrix, which is computationally intractable for billion-scale models. Recent state-of-the-art methods like LESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and TRAK <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>)</cite> circumvent this bottleneck by projecting gradients into lower dimensions and approximating the Hessian inverse using optimizer statistics (e.g., Adam’s second moment). Critically, these methods rely on a <span id="A2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diagonal approximation</span> of the curvature. This implicitly assumes that model parameters are statistically independent and the optimization landscape is axis-aligned.
Unlike prior optimizer-based methods (e.g., LESS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>) that rely on intermediate optimizer states (such as Adam’s moments) to approximate influence, we posit that <span id="A2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">data selection should not be constrained by the efficiency-driven simplifications of specific optimizers</span>. Instead, it should aim to approximate the <span id="A2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ideal</span> Newton step determined by the underlying parameter geometry of the target task.
While optimizer states provide a computationally cheap diagonal approximation, they often fail to capture the coupled geometry inherent in PEFT fine-tuning.
The effectiveness of <span id="A2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> demonstrates that identifying and aligning with the <span id="A2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">principal optimization directions</span> of the target subspace is more critical than merely preserving gradient inner products or applying heuristic rescaling. By prioritizing directional consistency over magnitude reconstruction, <span id="A2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> marks a paradigm shift from optimizer-dependent heuristics to intrinsic geometric subspace recovery.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spectral Properties of Deep Optimization.</span> Our approach is grounded in the spectral analysis of neural network optimization. It is well-established that the Hessian and gradient covariance of deep networks exhibit a “bulk-and-outlier” or heavy-tailed spectral structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sagun et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papyan, 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghorbani et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. Specifically, the optimization trajectory is often confined to a low-dimensional manifold (low effective rank), while the remaining dimensions are dominated by stochastic noise <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2018a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2018b</a>)</cite>. Standard influence methods that attempt to invert the full curvature often inadvertently amplify this noise, particularly in the early stages of training. <span id="A2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> aligns with these insights by adopting a spectral filtering perspective: instead of unstable curvature inversion, we perform robust subspace projection. This connects data selection with the intrinsic dimension of the optimization trajectory, ensuring that selection is driven by stable signal components rather than noise.</p>
</div>
</section>

<td id="A3.T5.5.40.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;"><math id="A3.T5.m74" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}}^{(j)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Sim</mtext><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝒛</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝒛</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">val</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}}^{(j)})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A3.T5.5.40.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;">
<span id="A3.T5.5.40.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:255.3pt;">
<span id="A3.T5.5.40.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T5.5.40.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Subspace cosine similarity at checkpoint </span><math id="A3.T5.m75" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A3.T5.5.40.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> (Eq. (</span><a href="#S4.E16" title="Equation 16 ‣ 4.1 Subspace Gradient Feature Computation ‣ 4 GIST: The Proposed Methodology ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a><span id="A3.T5.5.40.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">))</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A3.T5.5.41" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T5.5.41.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;"><math id="A3.T5.m76" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{FinalScore}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">FinalScore</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝒛</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{FinalScore}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A3.T5.5.41.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:0.7pt;padding-bottom:0.7pt;">
<span id="A3.T5.5.41.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:255.3pt;">
<span id="A3.T5.5.41.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.T5.5.41.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Aggregated score for selection, </span><math id="A3.T5.m77" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{FinalScore}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i})=\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,J\}}\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}}^{(j)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">FinalScore</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝒛</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">max</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em" mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">J</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mtext mathsize="0.900em">Sim</mtext><mi mathsize="0.900em">t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝒛</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi></msub><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.900em">𝒛</mi><mi mathsize="0.900em">val</mi><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">(</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">j</mi><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{FinalScore}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i})=\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,J\}}\text{Sim}_{t}(\boldsymbol{z}_{i},\boldsymbol{z}_{\mathrm{val}}^{(j)})</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
