<p id="A5.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text">Let <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{A}\triangleq\mathrm{vec}(A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mi>vec</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{A}\triangleq\mathrm{vec}(A)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>-block of parameters.
From (<a href="#A5.E39" title="Equation 39 ‣ Proof. ‣ E.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">39</span></a>), the <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(A_{kj_{1}},A_{kj_{2}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(A_{kj_{1}},A_{kj_{2}})</annotation></semantics></math> Hessian entry equals</span></p>

<p id="A5.SS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text">Using (<a href="#A5.E42" title="Equation 42 ‣ Proof. ‣ E.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">42</span></a>) for <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j=j_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j=j_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j=j_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j=j_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> yields</span></p>

<p id="A5.SS2.p6.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p6.3.1" class="ltx_text">which is exactly Eq. (<a href="#A5.E37" title="Equation 37 ‣ Proof. ‣ E.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">37</span></a>).
Therefore, if the <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math>-space curvature <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{W}</annotation></semantics></math> couples the two directions
<math id="A5.SS2.p6.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="e_{j_{1}}\otimes B_{:k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{j_{1}}\otimes B_{:k}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS2.p6.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="e_{j_{2}}\otimes B_{:k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><msub><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><mi>B</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{j_{2}}\otimes B_{:k}</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., the quadratic form is nonzero),
then the LoRA-parameter Hessian has a nonzero off-diagonal entry.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text">The same argument applies to <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>.
For <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in[d_{\mathrm{out}}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>out</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in[d_{\mathrm{out}}]</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\in[r]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\in[r]</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{(i,k)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>F</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{(i,k)}</annotation></semantics></math> the matrix with a <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i,k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i,k)</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="A5.E45" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E45.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{\partial W}{\partial <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(45)</span></td></tr></tbody>

<p id="A5.SS2.p7.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p7.2.1" class="ltx_text">Hence</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E46.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial B_{i_{1}k}\,\partial B_{i_{2}k}}=\big(A_{k:}^{\top}\otimes e_{i_{1}}\big)^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{W}\big(A_{k:}^{\top}\otimes e_{i_{2}}\big)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mo>∂</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mi>W</mi></msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{L}}{\partial B_{i_{1}k}\,\partial B_{i_{2}k}}=\big(A_{k:}^{\top}\otimes e_{i_{1}}\big)^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{W}\big(A_{k:}^{\top}\otimes e_{i_{2}}\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A5.SS2.p7.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p7.3.1" class="ltx_text">and similarly for the mixed blocks <math id="A5.SS2.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(A,B)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(A,B)</annotation></semantics></math>.
∎</span></p>

<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Proof of Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a></h3>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Notation and definitions.</span>
A symmetric matrix <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> is <em id="A5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">positive semidefinite (PSD)</em> if
<math id="A5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐌𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{x}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For two <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspaces <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> with orthonormal bases
<math id="A5.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐕</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}</annotation></semantics></math>, the principal angles
<math id="A5.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})=\mathrm{diag}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{r})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})=\mathrm{diag}(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{r})</annotation></semantics></math> are defined by
<math id="A5.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos\theta_{i}=\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐕</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos\theta_{i}=\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{V})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes singular values.
We use <math id="A5.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\sin\Theta(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})\|_{2}=\sin\theta_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\sin\Theta(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})\|_{2}=\sin\theta_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> as the subspace distance.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
Let the validation objective be the average negative log-likelihood (NLL)</p>
<table id="A5.E47" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E47.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\ell_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}),\qquad\ell_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=-\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(y_{i}\mid x_{i})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>val</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>val</mi></msub></munderover><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\ell_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}),\qquad\ell_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=-\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(47)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Denote the validation Hessian
<math id="A5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="A5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> and
<math id="A5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{val}}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>val</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{val}}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> stack <math id="A5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{g}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐠</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝜽</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{g}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> as rows.
We define the empirical Fisher-type proxy</p>
<table id="A5.E48" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E48.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\triangleq\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>val</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\triangleq\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(48)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Note that Scaling by <math id="A5.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/n_{\mathrm{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>val</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/n_{\mathrm{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> does not affect eigenspaces.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_assumption">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Assumption E.1</span></span><span id="A5.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Eigenspace separation)<span id="A5.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A5.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="A5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{1}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.1389em">⋯</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em">≥</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{1}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{d}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Assume the top-<math id="A5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> eigenspace of <math id="A5.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> is separated by an eigengap</p>

<div id="A5.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma E.2</span></span><span id="A5.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Gauss–Newton/Fisher decomposition for NLL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papyan, 2020</a>)</cite>)<span id="A5.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Consider an NLL objective <math id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})=-\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(y\mid x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})=-\log p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(y\mid x)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under standard regularity assumptions (twice differentiability and interchange of derivatives),
the Hessian admits the decomposition</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(50)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}(\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> is a Fisher/Gauss–Newton-type PSD curvature term,
and <math id="A5.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐑</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta})</annotation></semantics></math> collects residual curvature terms involving second derivatives of the model map
(e.g., the “non-Gauss–Newton” component).
Consequently, for the validation objective,</span></p>

<div id="A5.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma E.3</span></span><span id="A5.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Davis–Kahan Theorem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davis and Kahan, 1970</a>)</cite>)<span id="A5.Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> be symmetric, and let
<math id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{A})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{B})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{B})</annotation></semantics></math> denote their top-<math id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> eigenspaces.
Assume <math id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> has an eigengap <math id="A5.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{B})-\lambda_{r+1}(\mathbf{B})&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=\lambda_{r}(\mathbf{B})-\lambda_{r+1}(\mathbf{B})&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then</span></p>
<table id="A5.E52" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E52.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{A}),\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{B})\big)\big\|_{2}\ \leq\ \frac{\|\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}\|_{2}}{\gamma}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐁</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.778em" rspace="0.778em">≤</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>γ</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{A}),\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{B})\big)\big\|_{2}\ \leq\ \frac{\|\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{B}\|_{2}}{\gamma}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(52)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a></span> (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). <span id="A5.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="A5.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{M})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐌</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{M})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the top-<math id="A5.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> eigenspace of a PSD matrix <math id="A5.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐌</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Assume Assumption <a href="#A5.Thmtheorem1" title="Assumption E.1 (Eigenspace separation). ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.
For NLL objectives, let <math id="A5.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> be the validation Hessian and
<math id="A5.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>val</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="A5.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> be a Fisher/Gauss–Newton-type curvature term from Lemma <a href="#A5.Thmtheorem2" title="Lemma E.2 (Gauss–Newton/Fisher decomposition for NLL ( , )). ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>,
so that <math id="A5.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}+\mathbf{R}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}+\mathbf{R}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Define</span></p>
<table id="A5.E53" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E53.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{t}\triangleq\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}+\|\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}-\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\|_{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{t}\triangleq\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}+\|\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}-\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\|_{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(53)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Then the dominant subspaces are close:</span></p>
<table id="A5.E54" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E54.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}),\ \mathcal{S}_{r}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\big)\big\|_{2}\ \leq\ \frac{\varepsilon_{t}}{\gamma_{t}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.778em" rspace="0.778em">≤</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}),\ \mathcal{S}_{r}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\big)\big\|_{2}\ \leq\ \frac{\varepsilon_{t}}{\gamma_{t}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(54)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A5.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">By Lemma <a href="#A5.Thmtheorem2" title="Lemma E.2 (Gauss–Newton/Fisher decomposition for NLL ( , )). ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>, we have the decomposition</span></p>
<table id="A5.E55" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E55.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}+\mathbf{R}_{t}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐅</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{val},t}+\mathbf{R}_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(55)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>

<table id="A5.E56" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
<p id="A5.SS3.p5.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p5.3.1" class="ltx_text">Taking operator norms and applying the triangle inequality yields</span></p>
<table id="A5.E57" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

</table>
<p id="A5.SS3.p5.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p5.4.1" class="ltx_text">Under Assumption <a href="#A5.Thmtheorem1" title="Assumption E.1 (Eigenspace separation). ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>, <math id="A5.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> has an eigengap <math id="A5.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{t}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{t}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> at rank <math id="A5.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>.
Applying Lemma <a href="#A5.Thmtheorem3" title="Lemma E.3 (Davis–Kahan Theorem ( , )). ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a> with
<math id="A5.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐀</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}=\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐁</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐅</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}=\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> gives</span></p>
<table id="A5.E58" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E58.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\big\|\sin\Theta\big(\mathcal{S}_{r}(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}),\ \mathcal{S}_{r}(\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t})\big)\big\|_{2}\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{val},t}-\widehat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathrm{val},t}\|_{2}}{\gamma_{t}}\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{t}}{\gamma_{t}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐇</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mover <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>

<p id="A5.SS3.p5.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS3.p5.5.1" class="ltx_text">which proves the claim.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A5.Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A5.Thmtheorem4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Remark E.4</span></span><span id="A5.Thmtheorem4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> </span>(Theoretical Necessity of Warmup)<span id="A5.Thmtheorem4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></h6>
<div id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> establishes that the fidelity of our subspace recovery is bounded by the ratio <math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{t}/\gamma_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{t}/\gamma_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. At initialization (<math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=0</annotation></semantics></math>), the high negative log-likelihood implies a large non-Gauss-Newton residual term <math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (inflating <math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>) and a chaotic gradient spectrum with a negligible eigengap <math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Therefore, a lightweight warmup is not merely a heuristic but a theoretical prerequisite. It drives the optimization trajectory into a local basin where the residual curvature decays (<math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, validating the Gauss-Newton approximation <math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{H}\approx\mathbf{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐇</mi><mo>≈</mo><mi>𝐅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{H}\approx\mathbf{F}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the intrinsic task-specific structure emerges (maximizing <math id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>γ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>). This ensures <span id="A5.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> operates in a regime where the empirical proxy is mathematically guaranteed to align with the true Hessian geometry.</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Baseline Details</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide detailed implementation specifications for all baseline methods compared in our experiments. We categorize these methods into four groups: Random Selection, Hardness-aware Heuristics, Similarity-based Methods, and Optimizer-based Methods.
For baseline approaches that involve stochasticity, we perform three runs with different random seeds and report the average performance and standard deviation.</p>
</div>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Random Selection</h3>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ <span id="A6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random Selection</span> as a standard baseline, which uniformly samples data points from the candidate pool <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> until the target budget <math id="A6.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> is met. Despite its simplicity, random selection often serves as a strong baseline in instruction tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Random.</span>
We uniformly sample data points from the entire candidate pool <math id="A6.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> until the budget is met.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Hard Example Mining</h3>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These methods select data based on intrinsic properties of the examples (e.g., difficulty or length), independent of the specific target task. In our geometric view (Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), these methods typically prioritize gradient magnitude over direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Length.</span>
We sort examples by length (in tokens) and take the longest samples. This has been shown to be a strong baseline by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and is computationally cheap, only requiring computing the length of each sample in our data pool.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Perplexity (PPL).</span>
We compute the loss (perplexity) of each sample <math id="A6.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\in\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\in\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> using the pre-trained base model, following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin and Rush, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Antonello et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marion et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ankner et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yin and Rush (2025)</a></cite>, we select samples with the highest loss values (hardest samples).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Similarity-based Methods</h3>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These methods select training samples <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\in\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\in\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> that are semantically close to the target validation examples <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embedding.</span>
Following standard practices in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we employ the <span id="A6.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GTR-Base</span> model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2022</a>)</cite> as the external encoder.
For every candidate sample <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> and validation sample <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute their embeddings using GTR-Base and calculate the cosine similarity score. The final score for a candidate <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is its maximum similarity to any example in the validation set.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RDS+.</span>
We adopt the <span id="A6.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RDS+</span> method proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
Unlike standard embedding approaches, RDS+ utilizes the base model’s own internal representations to measure similarity.
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ivison et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we extract the hidden states from the last layer and apply a position-weighted mean pooling to derive the representation for each sequence. This weighted pooling strategy is designed to better capture the instruction-following semantics compared to standard mean pooling.
We use the official codebase provided by the authors<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/hamishivi/automated-instruction-selection" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/hamishivi/automated-instruction-selection</a></span></span></span> for implementation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Optimizer-based Methods</h3>

<div id="A6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These methods estimate the gradient-based influence of training samples derived from optimizer statistics (e.g., Adam’s
second-moment estimates on the validation loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LESS.</span>
We follow the procedure outlined in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>. We first train an auxiliary LoRA model on a random subset of the data. Then, we compute the influence score for each pair <math id="A6.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(v,d)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(v,d)</annotation></semantics></math> using gradient projections.
Crucially, LESS utilizes the optimizer states (Adam’s moments) to re-scale gradients.
We use the official codebase provided by the authors<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/princeton-nlp/LESS" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/princeton-nlp/LESS</a></span></span></span> for implementation.
We follow the paper’s default setup, using 4 epochs and setting the random projection dimension to 8192. Also we adopt the reported performance of LESS on Llama2-7B from the original paper.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Training</h2>

<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>Training Datasets</h3>

<div id="A7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the same four preprocessed training datasets as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023)</a></cite>. All are human-written or human-annotated; details are provided in <a href="#A7.T6" title="In G.1 Training Datasets ‣ Appendix G Training ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. <span id="A7.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">flan v2</span> and <span id="A7.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">cot</span> are derived from existing NLP benchmarks, whereas <span id="A7.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">dolly</span> and <span id="A7.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">open assistant 1</span> contain open-ended generation examples with human-written responses. These datasets differ substantially in format, length, and task type, highlighting the diversity of instruction-tuning data. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023)</a></cite>, we standardize them using the same “Tulu” format.</p>
</div>

<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Infrastructure and Implementation. </h3>

<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments were conducted on a system equipped with NVIDIA A100 GPU and AMD EPYC 7473X 24-core processor (48 threads).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.3 </span>Training Details</h3>

<div id="A7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt the training configuration from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>. We implemented parameter-efficient fine-tuning across all experiments using LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Training was performed for 4 epochs with a batch size of 128, utilizing a learning rate scheduler that combines linear warm-up with cosine decay, peaking at <math id="A7.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\times 10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>.For the LoRA configuration, we targeted all attention matrices with a rank of 128, <math id="A7.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=512</annotation></semantics></math>, and a dropout rate of 0.1. This setup resulted in 135M trainable parameters (<math id="A7.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.95\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.95</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.95\%</annotation></semantics></math>) for Llama2-7B, 73M (<math id="A7.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.23\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.23</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.23\%</annotation></semantics></math>) for Llama3.2-3B, and 34M (<math id="A7.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.21\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.21</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.21\%</annotation></semantics></math>) for Qwen2.5-1.5B.To ensure robustness, each experiment was repeated over three trials using distinct random seeds. For random selection baselines, this involved sampling three unique subsets from the training data. For our proposed method, distinct subsets were selected from separate models that had undergone warmup training on varied data partitions. Optimization seeds remained consistent throughout all experiments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>Evaluation</h2>

<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2023)</a></cite> to evaluate the performance of the models on the target tasks. For <span id="A8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span>, we measure the 5-shot accuracy of the test set averaged across 57 subtasks. For <span id="A8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span>, we measure the 1-shot macro-averaged F1 score across all 11 languages. We adopt the gold-passage setup where one passage containing the reference answer is provided to the model. For <span id="A8.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span>, we report the average 3-shot exact match score across all tasks. Chain-of-thought reasoning is provided in each in-context learning example to prompt the model to generate chain-of-thought reasoning traces for test examples. We evaluate on the validation set <math id="A8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}</annotation></semantics></math> (the same reference set used for data selection) at the end of each epoch and select the best checkpoint to evaluate on the final test set for each experiment. Note that this procedure might introduce some bias to the final test set, given that the validation set is relatively small (e.g., <span id="A8.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> only has 9 validation examples in total). According to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al. (2024)</a></cite>, this bias doesn’t affect the comparisons between different methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>More Experiment Results</h2>

<section id="A9.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.1 </span>Gradient Spectrum Analysis</h3>

<figure id="A9.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F6.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="A9.F6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Spectral Analysis of Gradient Subspaces across Models and Epochs.<span id="A9.F6.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
</span>Top Row:<span id="A9.F6.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Singular value spectra (log scale) of the gradient covariance matrix. Early epochs (blue solid lines) show slower decay, indicating a higher-dimensional optimization landscape.
</span>Bottom Row:<span id="A9.F6.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Cumulative explained variance. Later epochs (dotted red lines) reach 95% variance with fewer components, signaling dimensional shrinkage.
Notably, larger models (e.g., Llama2-7B) exhibit a slower spectral decay compared to smaller counterparts, reflecting a higher intrinsic dimensionality for task adaptation.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A9.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A9.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Early training stages preserve a higher effective dimension, while larger models exhibit richer intrinsic structures.</span> Figure <a href="#A9.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ I.1 Gradient Spectrum Analysis ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> visualizes the spectral properties of the target gradient covariance matrices across different training epochs and model architectures. First, we observe that earlier epochs (e.g., Epoch 1) consistently exhibit a “heavier tail” in their singular value distribution compared to later epochs. As training progresses, the spectrum decays more rapidly, and the cumulative variance rises sharper, indicating a collapse of the optimization trajectory into a lower-dimensional subspace. This suggests that the “warm-up” stage contains diverse and exploratory gradient signals crucial for robust data selection, whereas later stages become over-specialized.
Regarding model scale, models with larger parameter counts demonstrate a higher intrinsic dimension. By comparing the singular value decay rates, larger models maintain significant singular values across a wider range of components, whereas smaller models show a faster spectral drop-off. This implies that larger models rely on a more complex and high-dimensional feature subspace for task adaptation, necessitating a rank-adaptive selection strategy like <span id="A9.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>.</p>
</div>
