</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F7.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A9.F7.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Impact of Dataset Scale and Task Type on Gradient Geometry.<span id="A9.F7.11.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We analyze the spectral properties of Llama3.2-3B gradients across three datasets with varying sizes.
</span>Top Row:<span id="A9.F7.11.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Singular value spectra show that intrinsic dimension scales with data size. <span id="A9.F7.11.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> exhibits a smooth, heavy-tailed decay, whereas <span id="A9.F7.11.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> suffers from extreme spectral sparsity due to data scarcity.
</span>Bottom Row:<span id="A9.F7.11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Cumulative explained variance. Note that across all scales, </span>Epoch 1 (blue solid lines) consistently preserves a higher effective dimension<span id="A9.F7.11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> (slower variance saturation) compared to later epochs (red dotted lines). This confirms that early-stage gradients are essential for preventing subspace collapse, especially in low-resource regimes like <span id="A9.F7.11.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span>.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A9.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A9.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spectral filtering is essential to counteract subspace underspecification in low-resource regimes.</span>
Figure <a href="#A9.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ I.1 Gradient Spectrum Analysis ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reveals a critical disparity in gradient geometry across data scales.
While the data-rich <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> exhibits a smooth, heavy-tailed singular value distribution (indicating a well-covered feature space), <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> and <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> display marked spectral sparsity.
Specifically, for these smaller datasets, the limited sample size is insufficient to span the effective optimization subspace.
Unlike <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span>, the eigenvalues of <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> and <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> decrease precipitously, indicating that the empirical geometry is severely rank-deficient.
Consequently, the vast majority of the parameter space collapses into the null space of the empirical estimator.
In this underspecified regime, any full-rank approximation (like diagonal inversion) would be ill-posed: the variance of the preconditioner would be erroneously dominated by these null-space directions (where curvature is near-zero and inversion explodes), amplifying noise rather than signal.
This observation fundamentally justifies <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>’s <span id="A9.SS1.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spectral filtering</span>:
we must rigorously filter for the dominant principal components to recover the valid subspace, explicitly discarding the noisy null space to prevent subspace collapse.</p>
</div>
<div id="A9.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A9.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adaptive Rank Selection Strategy.</span>
To determine the optimal subspace rank <math id="A9.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> across diverse tasks, we adopt a <span id="A9.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">spectral-thresholding strategy with a few-shot safety constraint</span>.
Generally, we define the rank <math id="A9.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> as the minimum number of components required to capture 95% of the spectral variance of the gradient covariance matrix (calibrated on Llama2-7B). However, for extremely low-resource tasks, we introduce a full-rank retention rule to prevent information loss due to estimation variance.
Specifically:</p>
<ul id="A9.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:0.25cm;">
<li id="A9.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A9.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU<span id="A9.I1.i1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> (<math id="A9.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=150</annotation></semantics></math>):</span></span> The validation gradients exhibit a heavy-tailed distribution, requiring <math id="A9.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\approx 53\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>53</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 53\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the components (150 out of 285) to reach the 95% variance threshold, confirming the high intrinsic dimensionality of the task.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A9.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A9.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH<span id="A9.I1.i2.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> (<math id="A9.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=50</annotation></semantics></math>):</span></span> The spectrum saturates more rapidly. A rank of 50 captures the dominant 95% of signals (out of 81), effectively filtering out the tail components associated with optimization noise.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A9.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A9.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A9.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA<span id="A9.I1.i3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> (<math id="A9.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=9</annotation></semantics></math>):</span></span> Although the 95% variance threshold is met at <math id="A9.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\approx 5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\approx 5</annotation></semantics></math>, the absolute sample size (<math id="A9.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=9</annotation></semantics></math>) is critically small. In such <span id="A9.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">extreme few-shot regimes</span>, the statistical stability of spectral estimation is limited, and the computational cost of full-rank retention is negligible. Therefore, we override the threshold and retain the full rank (<math id="A9.I1.i3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=|\mathcal{D}_{\text{val}}|=9</annotation></semantics></math>) to ensure zero information loss.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="A9.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">This hybrid strategy balances theoretical rigor with practical robustness for data-scarce scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.2 </span>Warmup and Training Dynamics of LoRA Finetuning</h3>

<figure id="A9.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="A9.F8.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/qwen_270k_loss_vs_epoch.svg" id="A9.F8.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/358;" width="476" height="358"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F8.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="A9.F8.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Qwen2.5-1.5B (270k)</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="A9.F8.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/qwen_13.5k_loss_vs_epoch.svg" id="A9.F8.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/358;" width="476" height="358"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F8.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="A9.F8.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Qwen2.5-1.5B (13.5k)</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="A9.F8.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/llama3.2_13.5k_loss_vs_epoch.svg" id="A9.F8.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/358;" width="476" height="358"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F8.sf3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(c)</span> </span><span id="A9.F8.sf3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Llama3.2-3B (13.5k)</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_4">
<figure id="A9.F8.sf4" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18584v1/llama2_13.5k_loss_vs_epoch.svg" id="A9.F8.sf4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/358;" width="476" height="358"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F8.sf4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(d)</span> </span><span id="A9.F8.sf4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Llama2-7B (13.5k)</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A9.F8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="A9.F8.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Rapid loss convergence in the first epoch creates a stable geometric basin.<span id="A9.F8.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We observe consistent training dynamics across varying data scales (13.5k vs. 270k) and model architectures, where the loss drops precipitously within the initial phase (<math id="A9.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;0.5</annotation></semantics></math> epoch) before entering a bounded oscillatory regime.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A9.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To verify the assumptions underlying Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, we analyze the training dynamics of multiple instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2, Llama2) across different data scales. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#A9.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ I.2 Warmup and Training Dynamics of LoRA Finetuning ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we consistently observe a distinct two-phase phenomenon: a precipitous drop in loss within the first epoch, followed by a stable oscillatory regime. This behavior is critical for the validity of our spectral approximation. The rapid initial descent effectively minimizes the non-Gauss-Newton residual term <math id="A9.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>𝐑</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\mathbf{R}_{t}\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (Eq. (<a href="#A5.E57" title="Equation 57 ‣ Proof. ‣ E.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ Appendix E Theoretical Proof ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">57</span></a>)), fulfilling the prerequisite for the Fisher information to dominate the Hessian geometry. Furthermore, this transition aligns with the characterization of the Adam optimizer as an ”oscillator” in the later stages of training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Once the adaptive second-moment estimates <math id="A9.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> stabilize after the initial shock, the optimization trajectory becomes confined to a low-dimensional basin. In this regime, while the parameters may oscillate locally, the principal subspace of the gradients remains directionally consistent, thereby justifying our strategy of extracting geometric signals from the early-stabilized warmup checkpoints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.3 </span>Cross-Model Transferability</h3>

<div id="A9.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we ask <span id="A9.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">whether a subset selected by one model can also benefit other models</span>.
We denote by <span id="A9.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST-T</span> the transfer setting where we select data using Qwen2.5-1.5B and then fine-tune Llama2-7B and Llama3.2-3B on the selected subset; results are reported in Table <a href="#A9.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ I.3 Cross-Model Transferability ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.
Overall, transfer remains effective and consistently improves over the base model, but it is generally weaker than running <span id="A9.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> with the target model.
Interestingly, unlike <span id="A9.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> and <span id="A9.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span>, the performance drop on <span id="A9.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> is negligible under transfer.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T7.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 7</span>: </span><span id="A9.T7.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Main results with <span id="A9.T7.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> and transfer <span id="A9.T7.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST-T</span>.
<span id="A9.T7.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> selects 5% of training data using the target model itself.
<span id="A9.T7.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST-T</span> selects 5% data <em id="A9.T7.9.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">once</em> using Qwen2.5-1.5B and then reuses the same selected subset to fine-tune other models.</span></figcaption>

<section id="A9.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.4 </span>Ablation of Warmup Stage</h3>

<div id="A9.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because our analysis in Theorem <a href="#S3.Thmtheorem3" title="Theorem 3.3 (Eigenspace stability of the proxy). ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> relies on a Newton–Gauss decomposition of the Hessian, we clarify that a brief warmup phase is necessary to drive the loss to a sufficiently small regime. In this section, we empirically validate the importance of warmup. As shown in Table <a href="#A9.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ I.4 Ablation of Warmup Stage ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, <span id="A9.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> with a one-epoch warmup consistently outperforms its no-warmup variant across <span id="A9.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span>, <span id="A9.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span>, and <span id="A9.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>: </span><span id="A9.T8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Warmup ablation on Llama3.2-3B under the same 5% selection budget. Removing warmup consistently degrades performance across tasks.</span></figcaption>
<div id="A9.T8.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:228.0pt;height:46.7pt;vertical-align:-21.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-6.0pt,1.2pt) scale(0.9,0.9) ;">
<table id="A9.T8.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A9.T8.5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

</section>
<section id="A9.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.5 </span>Influence of LoRA Rank</h3>

<div id="A9.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A9.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ I.5 Influence of LoRA Rank ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> reveals that <span id="A9.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> remains exceptionally robust under a tighter PEFT bottleneck (LoRA rank <math id="A9.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r{=}8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r{=}8</annotation></semantics></math> with 4.6M trainable parameters, accounting 0.14% for Llama3.2-3B), while the baseline LESS degrades noticeably. On <span id="A9.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span>, reducing the rank causes LESS to drop from 67.1% to 65.0%, whereas <span id="A9.SS5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> effectively retains its performance (67.5%), outperforming LESS by a clear margin. Remarkably, on <span id="A9.SS5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span>, <span id="A9.SS5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> at <math id="A9.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r{=}8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r{=}8</annotation></semantics></math> (48.4%) even slightly exceeds its own <math id="A9.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r{=}128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r{=}128</annotation></semantics></math> result (48.0%), confirming that our selected subsets are highly data-efficient.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T9.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 9</span>: </span><span id="A9.T9.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">LoRA rank ablation on Llama3.2-3B (5% selection budget).
We compare the robustness of <span id="A9.T9.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> against LESS under different LoRA rank constraints.
Our method (<span id="A9.T9.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>) maintains significant gains even in the low-rank setting (<math id="A9.T9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r{=}8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r{=}8</annotation></semantics></math>).
Gray scripts denote standard deviations across 3 runs.</span></figcaption>

<td id="A9.T9.7.1.6.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;"><span id="A9.T9.7.1.6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">48.0<math id="A9.T9.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" mathsize="0.700em">±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math></span><span id="A9.T9.7.1.6.5.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">0.5</span></td>
<td id="A9.T9.7.1.6.6" class="ltx_td" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;"></td>
<td id="A9.T9.7.1.6.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;">46.1<math id="A9.T9.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#808080;" mathcolor="#808080" mathsize="0.700em">±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A9.T9.7.1.6.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">0.6</span></td>

<tr id="A9.T9.7.1.7" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A9.T9.7.1.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;"><span id="A9.T9.7.1.7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Average</span></th>

<td id="A9.T9.7.1.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;">56.6</td>
<td id="A9.T9.7.1.7.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;"><span id="A9.T9.7.1.7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">57.8</span></td>
<td id="A9.T9.7.1.7.6" class="ltx_td ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;"></td>
<td id="A9.T9.7.1.7.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;">55.8</td>
<td id="A9.T9.7.1.7.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 8.0pt;"><span id="A9.T9.7.1.7.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">57.0</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="A9.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that <span id="A9.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">reducing LoRA rank amplifies parameter coupling</span>: updates are constrained to a narrower bilinear subspace, making the optimization geometry more “rotated” and less axis-aligned. Methods relying on diagonal surrogates (like LESS) struggle to represent this coupled geometry and thus become sensitive to rank reduction. In contrast, <span id="A9.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> scores examples via alignment within a task-specific subspace extracted from validation gradients. This approach inherently preserves cross-parameter structures, allowing <span id="A9.SS5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> to identify high-value training signals that remain effective even when the trainable degrees of freedom are heavily restricted.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">I.6 </span>Influence of Tail Principle Directions</h3>

<div id="A9.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A9.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ I.6 Influence of Tail Principle Directions ‣ Appendix I More Experiment Results ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> compares <span id="A9.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> against a tail-only variant (<span id="A9.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST-tail</span>) under the same 5% selection budget.
While, in optimization view, directions associated with the smallest eigenvalues (tail components) can in principle yield the largest instantaneous decrease in the validation loss, they are also the most vulnerable to overfitting the validation signal and to stochastic gradient noise.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A9.T10" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A9.T10.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 10</span>: </span><span id="A9.T10.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Tail ablation on Llama3.2-3B under the same 5% selection budget. While <span id="A9.T10.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> consistently improves over <span id="A9.T10.8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Base</span> and <span id="A9.T10.8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Random</span>, selecting only the smallest principal direction (<span id="A9.T10.8.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST-tail</span>) can be unstable and may hurt task performance.</span></figcaption>

<div id="A9.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, <span id="A9.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span> is consistently strong across tasks, whereas <span id="A9.SS6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST-tail</span> exhibits highly task-dependent behavior: it is competitive on <span id="A9.SS6.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">MMLU</span> (56.4 vs. 56.1), but drops substantially on <span id="A9.SS6.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> (63.1 vs. 69.2) and collapses on <span id="A9.SS6.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">BBH</span> (38.5 vs. 48.0).
These results suggest that relying only on the decrease of validation loss is brittle, and motivate <em id="A9.SS6.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">automatically</em> selecting (or weighting) principal directions in a task-adaptive manner, which we leave as an important direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A10" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix J </span>Target Set Subspace Analysis</h2>

<div id="A10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since the task projector for <span id="A10.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> in our experiments maps original gradients to a low-dimensional subspace (specifically, a 9-dimensional space), we employ <span id="A10.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> on Qwen2.5-1.5B as a tractable case study to analyze the semantic distribution of subsets selected along each principal direction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A10.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, utilizing the compact SVD from Eq. (<a href="#S3.E13" title="Equation 13 ‣ 3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>), we decompose the Gram matrix as <math id="A10.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}=V_{r}\Sigma_{r}^{2}V_{r}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}^{\top}\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}=V_{r}\Sigma_{r}^{2}V_{r}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>. As established in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 The Solution: Optimal Geometry Recovery via Spectral Filtering ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>, we adopt this matrix as a first-order surrogate for the Hessian, implying <math id="A10.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\text{val},t}\approx V_{r}\Lambda V_{r}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\text{val},t}\approx V_{r}\Lambda V_{r}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> (where <math id="A10.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda\approx\Sigma_{r}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mo>≈</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda\approx\Sigma_{r}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>). Consequently, the pseudoinverse <math id="A10.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mtext>val</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>†</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\text{val},t}^{\dagger}</annotation></semantics></math> within the influence function (Eq. (<a href="#S3.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Theorem 3.1 (Single-level Approximate Optimization). ‣ 3.1 A Unified Optimization View of Data Selection ‣ 3 Theoretical Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>)) is approximated by <math id="A10.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{r}\Lambda^{-1}V_{r}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{r}\Lambda^{-1}V_{r}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A10.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From an optimization perspective, this spectral analysis highlights a <span id="A10.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">critical trade-off</span> between theoretical acceleration and empirical robustness. The leading principal directions (associated with larger singular values of <math id="A10.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math>) correspond to <span id="A10.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">dominant consensus patterns</span> with a high signal-to-noise ratio. While these directions ensure reliable descent, they typically contribute to smaller step updates due to high curvature constraints. Conversely, the trailing directions theoretically offer the potential for larger loss reductions (attributable to the inverse scaling effect of <math id="A10.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> in the influence approximation). However, in practice, these directions are often dominated by <span id="A10.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">stochastic gradient noise</span> and estimation errors, rendering them unreliable for generalization despite their theoretical efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="A10.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A10.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix J Target Set Subspace Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> illustrates the most influential training examples retrieved along distinct principal directions for a sample Telugu QA instance from the validation set. The English translation of the Telugu query is provided below:</p>
</div>
<div id="A10.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A10.p5.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="236.42" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 236.42" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,236.42) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 230.52 C 0 233.78 2.64 236.42 5.91 236.42 L 471.47 236.42 C 474.73 236.42 477.38 233.78 477.38 230.52 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 230.52 C 1.97 232.69 3.73 234.45 5.91 234.45 L 471.47 234.45 C 473.65 234.45 475.41 232.69 475.41 230.52 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.47)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:31.37em;--ltx-fo-height:14.9em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="208.86" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 206.17)" width="434.07"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A10.p5.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:31.37em;">
<span id="A10.p5.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.p5.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">&lt;|user|&gt;<span id="A10.p5.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> 
<br class="ltx_break">Context: Pātapāḍēru is a village in Paderu Mandal, Visakhapatnam district. It is 0 km from the mandal headquarters Paderu and 76 km from the nearest town Anakapalli. According to the 2011 Indian Census, the village has 830 households, a population of 3,687, and covers 268 hectares. The number of males is 1,398 and the number of females is 2,289. The Scheduled Castes population is 26, and the Scheduled Tribes population is 2,944. The census location code is 584655. PIN code: 531077.
<br class="ltx_break">Question: How many females were there in Pātapāḍēru village in 2011?

<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break"></span>&lt;|assistant|&gt;<span id="A10.p5.pic1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> 
<br class="ltx_break">2,289</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="A10.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Surprisingly, Table <a href="#A10.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix J Target Set Subspace Analysis ‣ GIST: Targeted Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Coupled Optimization Geometry" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> reveals that the samples selected by individual principal directions of <math id="A10.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐆</mi><mrow><mi>val</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{val},t}</annotation></semantics></math> exhibit a distinct hierarchy of task levels.
As previously discussed, leading principal directions represent high-confidence descent directions that, while contributing to smaller loss reductions, align with fundamental and general-purpose language tasks.
For instance, PC1 retrieves sentiment analysis reviews, while PC2 selects multi-step multiple-choice questions (MCQs), indicative of general reasoning capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A10.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, trailing directions target more granular and specific tasks, such as fact-checking (PC8) and non-English sentences (PC9).
While incorporating data along these directions yields larger loss reductions on the validation set, these directions are also more prone to falling into the null space.
Consequently, such aggressive loss reductions may stem from overfitting, potentially detrimental to generalization.
We observe that these semantic patterns across different principal directions remain consistent among the top-scoring samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A10.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A10.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Ultimately, when aggregating all principal directions for selection, the retrieved data semantically converges toward the validation example, heavily favoring Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks.
It also captures specific translation examples; notably, sample (4) <span id="A10.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">flan_v2_79833</span> explicitly selects an English-to-Telugu translation pair.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<figure id="A10.T11" class="ltx_table ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 11: </span>We use one Telugu <span id="A10.T11.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">TydiQA</span> validation instance to retrieve the most relevant training examples under <span id="A10.T11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GIST</span>.
Target Projector (nine principal directions) is precomputed via SVD on the original target set and reused here. For each direction, candidate examples are scored by their projection-based alignment, and the highest-scoring examples are retrieved. We then aggregate the nine directional scores to obtain a single overall score per example, and report the <span id="A10.T11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top-5</span> examples with the largest aggregated scores.</figcaption>

<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A10.T11.p12.2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Reasoning: Tom served on Monday to </span><math id="A10.T11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8\times 10=80" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">10</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">80</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8\times 10=80</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T11.p12.2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> clients. So Tom earned </span><math id="A10.T11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20/100\times 80=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">20</mn><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">100</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">80</mn></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">=</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20/100\times 80=16</annotation></semantics></math><span id="A10.T11.p12.2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> bonus points.</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A10.T11.p12.2.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Answer: 16</span>

<br class="ltx_break">
</span>
<span id="A10.T11.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A10.T11.p11.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T11.p11.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Assistant:</span><span id="A10.T11.p11.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> In a company, an employee earns bonus points equal to 20% of the number of customers served. Tom served 10 customers per hour for 8 hours on Monday. How many bonus points did Tom earn?</span></span>
</span></span></td></tr>

<br class="ltx_break">
<span id="A10.T11.p16.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T11.p16.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">User:</span><span id="A10.T11.p16.2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> Decide whether each claim is a factual statement.</span>

<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A10.T11.p16.2.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Answer: Yes.</span>
<br class="ltx_break"></span>

Options: yes / no / it is not possible to tell.</span></span>

<span id="A10.T11.p21" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A10.T11.p21.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T11.p21.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(2) cot_28147 — NLI question reconstruction

<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A10.T11.p21.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Assistant:</span><span id="A10.T11.p21.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> Q: Given the sentence “A man playing his music for a crowd.” can we conclude “A crowd gathers while a man plays a slow jam.”?
Options: yes / it is not possible to tell / no.
A: it is not possible to tell.</span></span>

<span id="A10.T11.p22" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="A10.T11.p22.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T11.p22.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(3) flan_v2_78693 — False-belief story QA
<br class="ltx_break">User:</span><span id="A10.T11.p22.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> You will be given a definition of a task first, then some input of the task.Given a story, answer the question about the story. The question is the last sentence in the input. These stories can be difficult due to their length and how each story has at least one of the three following scenarios: the first is when the individual’s belief matches reality, the second is when the individual’s belief does not match reality, and the third is when an individual has a false belief about another individual’s beliefs. The question will ask about the location of an object in the story with respect to either none or one of the three scenarios. Note that there are distractor sentences in each story that are unrelated to the question and are designed to confuse the reader. Logan entered the living_room. Ethan entered the living_room. The banana is in the red_crate. Logan moved the banana to the red_cupboard. Logan entered the cellar. Avery entered the cellar. The pumpkin is in the red_envelope. Logan moved the pumpkin to the blue_suitcase. Phone rang. Abigail entered the kitchen. Ethan entered the kitchen. The cabbage is in the green_cupboard. Abigail moved the cabbage to the red_drawer. Logan is in the cellar. Abigail entered the cellar. Phone rang. The pumpkin is in the blue_suitcase. Logan moved the pumpkin to the red_envelope. Where does Logan think that Abigail searches for the pumpkin? Output:</span>
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A10.T11.p22.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Assistant:</span><span id="A10.T11.p22.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> red_envelope</span></span>
</span>

<span id="A10.T11.p23.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A10.T11.p23.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">(4) flan_v2_79833 — English <math id="A10.T11.p23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> Telugu
